writing_guide: Scenarios are made up for practice. No patient names, dates of birth, addresses or incident numbers.
Simple and straightforward: a provider should know what's being asked within three seconds.
context: one short line of facts the question needs. Leave it out if the prompt says enough.
prompt: a plain question, 12 words or fewer. Spot questions say exactly what to tap: 'Tap the sentence…', 'Tap the vitals row…', 'Tap the med entry…'.
quote: chart text being judged. It shows in an 'As charted' box — never put chart text inside a quoted sentence.
Swipe statements: one plain claim, 12 words or fewer, not an instruction. Mix true and false, and avoid double negatives.
explain: two sentences at most. Lead with the rule, then why it matters.
spot charts: one clear problem. Vitals rows use time, hr, bp, rr, spo2 and optional pain; leave a value out to show it was not recorded.
Wrong options are mistakes crews really make, not throwaways. The right answer should not usually be the longest one.
Options: 3 or 4, each short enough to read in one glance.
source: where the fact comes from (GMR ImageTrend training, a regulation). The review page shows it; the game doesn't.

sign.name: Sign Last
sign.tip: Your crew signature goes on last, after handoff. Patient and ABA signatures are captured at the bedside.

vitals.name: Abnormal Vitals
vitals.tip: Abnormal is never 'stable.' Recheck it, chart it, report it.

fullset.name: Full Set Every Time
fullset.tip: HR, BP, RR, SpO2 and mental status on every set, and recheck after every treatment.

impression.name: Impression Matcher
impression.tip: The impression is why they needed an ambulance, and it must match what you charted.

meds.name: Dose Detective
meds.tip: Drug, dose, units, route, time — for every med, including ones given before you arrived.

psych.name: Psych Pro
psych.tip: Legal status, safety search, SI details, and who consented.

hospice.name: Code Status Keeper
hospice.tip: Code status, the DNR form, and why a car wouldn't do.

narrative.name: No Templates
narrative.tip: Write what you found, in plain objective words — not a checklist.

imt.name: ImageTrend Smarts
imt.tip: Sync, post, fix it in the Timeline, and pick the right box.

mn.name: Prove the Stretcher
mn.tip: Why an ambulance and not a car or wheelchair van. Show it with what you saw.

questions.prompt: You should add your crew signature before the chart is finished.
questions.explain: Your crew signature says the chart is complete and accurate. Add it last, after handoff.

questions.prompt: When should you add your crew signature?

options.text: After handoff, once the chart is complete
When you start the chart
At the bedside, with the patient's signature
Before you post the first time

questions.explain: Your crew signature goes on last. Patient and ABA signatures are captured at the bedside or at handoff.

questions.prompt: You can sign in your partner's place if they're busy.
questions.explain: Each crew member signs for themselves. Signing for a partner is a common error, and Clinical Education will ask for an addendum.
questions.source: GMR End User IMT: missing signatures (job aid)

questions.context: Your chart is finished and locked. Then you find a mistake.
questions.prompt: How do you fix it?

options.text: Ask Clinical Support to unlock it
Add an addendum in Elite Web
Fix it in Elite Field and post again
Start a new chart for the call

questions.explain: A locked chart is corrected by addendum in Elite Web. The original stays, and the addendum becomes part of the record.
questions.source: GMR End User IMT: Addendums; Elite Web

questions.prompt: What should you check before your crew signature?

options.text: The narrative is short
Your partner's name is spelled right
Narrative, vitals and meds all agree
The validation score reads 100

questions.explain: The chart has to agree with itself. A clean validation score means fields are filled in, not that they agree.

questions.context: 16-year-old going to a psychiatric facility.
questions.prompt: Tap the reading you should recheck.

narrative.text: Patient walked from bed to cot.
Report given to the receiving nurse.

questions.explain: 170/150 in a teenager is either an emergency or a bad reading — recheck it, manually if needed. Chart both readings and report it.

questions.prompt: A heart rate of 120 that never changes is 'stable.'
questions.explain: Stable means normal and unchanged. A steady 120 is tachycardia — chart it, what you did, and who you told.

questions.context: The patient's BP was 118/40.
questions.prompt: What's the best way to chart this?

options.text: Vitals stable.
BP 118/40. Alert, skin warm and dry; no complaints.
BP low, rechecked, patient fine. Reported to RN.
BP 118/40, rechecked 120/45. Alert, skin warm and dry. Reported to RN.

questions.explain: Name the abnormal number, show the recheck, and say who you told.

questions.prompt: A BP you took looks wrong. What do you do?

options.text: Recheck it and chart both readings
Replace it with the recheck
Delete it and take another
Chart only the one that looks right

questions.explain: Keep a reading you actually took, and chart the recheck beside it. A typo is different: open that entry and correct it.

questions.prompt: Tap the sentence that doesn't match the vitals.

narrative.text: On 2 L nasal cannula from the facility.
Report given to the receiving nurse.

questions.explain: SpO2 fell to 88% while heart and breathing rates rose — that isn't stable. Chart the change, what you did, and who you told.

questions.context: Patient got IV hydromorphone before you arrived.
questions.prompt: Tap the vitals row that's missing a value.

narrative.text: Hydromorphone 1 mg IV given in the ED at 1915.
Patient walked to the cot with one assist.

questions.explain: BP belongs in every set, especially after an opioid, when BP and breathing can drop. A blank BP looks like it was never checked.

questions.prompt: What's in a full set of vitals?

options.text: HR, BP, RR and SpO2
HR, BP, RR, SpO2 and mental status (GCS)
HR, BP and SpO2
Whatever the monitor sends, plus a pain score

questions.explain: GMR's standard includes mental status (GCS or LOC) with the vitals. Add a pain score when pain is part of the complaint.
questions.source: GMR End User IMT: Clinical Documentation Requirements

questions.prompt: If the patient refuses a BP, leave it blank.
questions.explain: Use the Pertinent Negative 'Refused' on the BP field. A blank looks like you skipped it and fails validation.
questions.source: GMR End User IMT: Pertinent Negatives

questions.context: Two-hour transfer. The patient is stable.
questions.prompt: Vitals at pickup and arrival are enough for this ride.
questions.explain: Recheck along the way and after any change or treatment. The 2026 guidelines set tighter intervals for some conditions, like BP every 5 minutes with ACS.

questions.prompt: After any treatment, including oxygen, take another set of vitals.
questions.explain: The recheck shows whether the treatment worked or caused harm. Chart the after as well as the before.

questions.context: Hospice patient. SpO2 69% on room air; you put on a non-rebreather.
questions.prompt: Which primary impression fits best?

options.text: Weakness
Pain
Respiratory Distress - Unspecified
No Apparent Illness/Injury (Adult)

questions.explain: Pick the problem that needed you — here, the low oxygen. A vague impression undersells why the patient needed an ambulance.

questions.context: Feeding tube came out at the nursing home. No pain or bleeding. Going to the ED to have it replaced.
questions.prompt: Which primary impression fits best?

options.text: No Apparent Illness/Injury (Adult)
Nausea / Vomiting
Weakness
Gastrointestinal System Issue (G.I.)

questions.explain: Chart the body system with the problem, then add 'Mechanical complication of … devices, implants and grafts' as a secondary impression. 'No Apparent Illness/Injury' contradicts an ambulance trip to the ED.

questions.prompt: Your impression shouldn't contradict your assessment or vitals.
questions.explain: 'Cardiac Dysrhythmia - Bradycardia' next to a charted heart rate of 75 doesn't hold up. The numbers and the impression should tell the same story.

questions.context: 16-year-old with suicidal thoughts and a plan. No attempt.
questions.prompt: Which primary impression fits best?

options.text: Behavioral / Psychiatric disorder
No Apparent Illness/Injury (Pediatric)
Anxiety/Emotional Upset
Suicide attempt

questions.explain: Thoughts with a plan are behavioral; 'Suicide attempt' is only for someone who acted. 'No Apparent Illness/Injury' undercuts why they needed you.

questions.prompt: When is 'No Apparent Illness/Injury' the right impression?

options.text: Whenever the patient is stable and has no new complaints
Almost never on an ambulance transfer
When you're not sure what to pick
On every routine transfer

questions.explain: Every ambulance transport has a reason. Chart that reason, even when the patient is stable.

questions.context: The nurse gave hydromorphone before you arrived.
questions.prompt: What's the best way to chart this?

options.text: RN gave Dilaudid .5 mg IV before EMS arrival.
Hydromorphone given by RN prior to arrival, dose per MAR.
RN gave hydromorphone 0.5 mg IV at 1415, before EMS arrival.
Pain meds given per RN.

questions.explain: Drug, dose, units, route, time. '.5' could mean mg or mL, and a missing leading zero is a setup for a tenfold error.

questions.prompt: Writing 0.5 mg is safer than writing .5 mg.
questions.explain: '.5' is easily misread as 5 — a tenfold error. Write 0.5 mg, and never a trailing zero like 5.0 mg.

questions.prompt: Meds given before you arrived don't go in your chart.
questions.explain: Enter them in the Medication power tool with Prior to Arrival set to match what happened. They change what to expect en route.
questions.source: GMR job aid: infusions already running on an IFT

questions.quote: ATIVAN AND HALDOL GIVEN FOR AGITATION.
questions.prompt: What's missing from this line?

options.text: Nothing
Brand names
The reason each was given and who ordered it
Dose, route and time for each

questions.explain: Sedatives change how you monitor the patient. Every med needs its dose, route and time.

questions.context: Patient leaving the ED after pain meds.
questions.prompt: Tap the med entry that's missing its dose.
questions.explain: 'Given twice' can't be checked by anyone. Every med needs drug, dose, route and time — like the other two lines.

questions.prompt: What belongs in every psych transfer chart?

options.text: Legal status: voluntary or involuntary
The patient's insurance
Your guess at the diagnosis
How long the patient waited in the ED for a bed

questions.explain: Chart legal status, the safety search, SI details, and who consented for a minor. Those protect the patient and you.

questions.context: Psych patient says they planned to use a knife.
questions.prompt: What must your chart show?

options.text: That the patient seemed calm and denied wanting to hurt anyone
That you did a safety search, and what you found
The patient's insurance
Nothing extra

questions.explain: A stated weapon plan makes the safety search essential. Chart that it was done and what turned up.

questions.context: Psych transfer.
questions.prompt: This line alone shows why the patient needed an ambulance.
questions.explain: On its own it suggests the opposite. Add the reason — for example, suicidal with a plan and needs 1:1 watch.

questions.context: Patient argued about going to the facility.
questions.prompt: What's the best way to chart this?

options.text: Leave it as written.
Pt combative and uncooperative with crew; eventually agreed to transport.
Pt yelling, refused to sit on cot. Explained the transfer; pt agreed and sat on cot.
Pt was difficult; calmed down after a while.

questions.explain: Describe what the patient said and did, what you did, and how it ended. A label like 'difficult' tells the next reader nothing.

questions.context: 12-year-old with suicidal thoughts. Mom is at the bedside.
questions.prompt: What should the chart say about consent?

options.text: Nothing — the hospital handles it
That the patient is a minor, checked on the billing page
Only needed if mom rides along
Who consented: name and relationship

questions.explain: For a minor, chart who consented and how they're related. That's the legal basis for the transport.

questions.prompt: Every hospice transport chart should list the code status.
questions.explain: If the patient declines en route, code status guides what you do. Note that the DNR form traveled with the patient.

questions.context: Hospice patient going home, too confused to decide. The family asks you not to take vitals.
questions.prompt: What do you chart?

options.text: Who declined, their relationship, and what you could see
Leave the vitals blank
Estimate the numbers
Take them anyway, and chart that the family objected to vitals

questions.explain: Use the Pertinent Negative 'Refused' and chart who declined and what you could see. If the patient can decide, ask them: family can't refuse for a patient who can.

questions.prompt: What belongs in every hospice transport chart?

options.text: The hospice agency's name, phone number and nurse on call
Code status, and that the DNR form came along
The family's opinion of the hospital
Nothing extra

questions.explain: Code status and the DNR form protect the patient's wishes if something changes en route.

questions.prompt: Hospice charts still need to say why an ambulance was needed.
questions.explain: Every transport needs a reason a car or wheelchair van wouldn't do, like being unable to sit in a wheelchair. Chart what you saw.

questions.prompt: What's the best way to chart this?

options.text: Pt transported home.
Hospice pt to home. DNR with pt. Pt bedbound, on home O2.
Hospice pt to home. DNR with pt. Can't get up or stand without 2 assist; can't sit in wheelchair.
Hospice transport home per family request; DNR on file.

questions.explain: Chart code status and what the patient can't do: get up, walk or sit in a wheelchair. 'Bedbound' and home O2 alone don't show an ambulance was needed.
questions.source: 42 CFR §410.40 (bed-confined)

questions.quote: ON SCENE, PRIMARY, SECONDARY, VITALS, PT TO COT.
questions.prompt: This is a complete narrative.
questions.explain: That's a checklist, not a narrative. It says you assessed, but not what you found.

questions.context: Hospital to a skilled nursing facility.
questions.prompt: Tap the line that's too vague.

narrative.text: Alert and oriented; skin warm and dry; breathing unlabored.
Report given to the receiving nurse at 1430.

questions.explain: 'Tolerated transport well' gives a reviewer nothing to check. Chart what you saw: mental status, breathing, pain and vitals.

questions.context: Your narrative says 'without incident' seven times.
questions.prompt: What's the fix?

options.text: Change each one to 'without issue' so it reads better
Delete the narrative
Leave it
Say it once; describe what you found

questions.explain: Swapping the phrase isn't a fix. The next caregiver needs what you observed.

questions.context: You meant to say the patient had no pain.
questions.quote: CREW STATED THEY DID NOT FEEL PAIN.
questions.prompt: What's the best way to chart this?

options.text: Patient denies pain.
Leave it as written.
No pain noted by crew.
They did not feel pain.

questions.explain: As written, it says the crew had no pain. Reread before you submit — who did what matters in a legal record.

questions.prompt: Quoting the patient's own words is good charting.
questions.explain: A direct quote like "my chest feels tight" is objective and hard to dispute. It beats your summary of what they meant.

questions.prompt: Which line is the most objective?

options.text: Pt was drunk.
Odor of alcohol, slurred speech, unsteady when standing.
Pt was intoxicated, belligerent and uncooperative with crew.
Pt obviously had too much.

questions.explain: Chart what you saw, heard and smelled. Labels like 'drunk' can be wrong and invite challenge.

questions.prompt: If sync is slow, you can close it and start charting.
questions.explain: Sync downloads current users, vehicles and validation rules. Close it early and you chart against old rules.
questions.source: GMR End User IMT: Elite Web v Elite Field (syncing)

questions.context: You finished a call but never posted.
questions.prompt: How long does Elite Field keep that chart?

options.text: Until you delete it
14 days
Up to 4 days
Forever, it backs itself up

questions.explain: Elite Field keeps unposted charts for only up to 4 days. Post early, post often: after a signature, after a CAD update, and before you close the chart.
questions.source: GMR End User IMT: Elite Web v Elite Field; Posting an Incident

questions.context: You can't find your chart in Elite Web.
questions.prompt: What do you check first?

options.text: File a Clinical Support ticket
Start a new chart
Ask your partner to rechart it
Whether you posted it

questions.explain: An unposted chart isn't in Web: look for the cloud icon and green check on the tablet home screen. If you posted with the wrong CAD, search Web by crew member.
questions.source: GMR End User IMT: Troubleshooting

questions.prompt: An auto-locked chart usually can't be unlocked; fix it with an addendum.
questions.explain: Unfinished charts auto-lock after 336 hours (14 days), and Clinical Support unlocks them only in narrow cases. Add corrections as an addendum in Elite Web.
questions.source: GMR End User IMT: What can Kayako do for you

questions.prompt: An entry in the Timeline shows in red. What does that mean?

options.text: It has a validation error you must fix
It has already posted
It's a warning to review before you finish
Your partner entered it

questions.explain: Red is a validation error and gold is a warning. Tap the arrow on the entry to open and fix it, and review the whole Timeline before you post.
questions.source: GMR End User IMT: Timeline

questions.context: A validation rule sends you to Procedures (Read Only) to fix an entry.
questions.prompt: Where do you fix it?

options.text: Type over it on the read-only tab
Open the entry in the Timeline
Delete the chart and start over
Explain it in the narrative instead

questions.explain: Medications and Procedures can't be edited on the read-only tabs. Edits to any Power Tool or Situation are made in the Timeline.
questions.source: GMR End User IMT: Read Only Tabs; Timeline

questions.context: Your patient's mental status changes en route.
questions.prompt: You should edit your first Assessment to show the new findings.
questions.explain: Add a new Assessment Power Tool for every reassessment after a change. Editing the first one erases what you found at pickup.
questions.source: GMR End User IMT: Assessments

questions.context: The patient can't tell you a date of birth and the facility doesn't have one.
questions.prompt: You can mark the Age field with a pertinent negative.
questions.explain: NEMSIS 3.5 rules don't allow a pertinent negative on age. Estimate the age instead; ages over 110 are rejected.
questions.source: GMR End User IMT: Patient Demographics

questions.context: The patient let you assess and take vitals, then refused transport.
questions.prompt: Which Patient Evaluation/Care choice fits?

options.text: Patient Refused Evaluation/Care
Patient Evaluated, No Care Required
Patient Evaluated and Refused Care
Patient Support Services Provided

questions.explain: You assessed them, so it's Evaluated and Refused Care; 'Refused Evaluation/Care' is for patients who refused before you assessed. Then set Crew and Transport dispositions so the refusal worksheet populates.
questions.source: GMR End User IMT: Dispositions, Patient Refused Medical Aid

questions.prompt: The ABA worksheet is required on every transport.
questions.explain: It appears under Signatures (ABA Navigation) whenever the patient was treated and transported. Its questions pick the right signature for you.
questions.source: GMR End User IMT: ABA Worksheet

questions.context: The patient can't sign and no authorized representative is present.
questions.prompt: Who signs the ABA?

options.text: Your partner signs on the patient's line as a witness
Nobody; post it unsigned
Skip the ABA since the patient couldn't sign
Your crew and a receiving-facility representative

questions.explain: The crew and the receiving facility co-sign. A chart with no signature at all needs a face sheet plus crew attestation, and that should be rare.
questions.source: GMR End User IMT: ABA Worksheet

questions.context: Your tablet died and the patient signed a paper ABA.
questions.prompt: What else does the chart need?

options.text: A crew member attestation in the ABA worksheet
Nothing; the paper form covers it
An electronic signature you enter for the patient
A note to mail the paper in later

questions.explain: A paper ABA needs a crew attestation in the worksheet, plus a clear photo of the form in Attachments. Paper is only for downtime or tablet failure.
questions.source: GMR End User IMT: Worksheets; ABA Worksheet; Trailing Documents

questions.prompt: CMS Level of Service should match the care you actually gave.
questions.explain: Pick from the definitions on screen based on the care given. The field doesn't set billing status, but it has to agree with the rest of the chart.
questions.source: GMR End User IMT: CMS Level of Service

questions.context: Hospital-to-rehab transfer. This is what's in the interfacility justification box.
questions.prompt: What's the best way to chart this?

options.text: Higher level of care needed per MD; patient accepted at receiving facility.
Pt needs inpatient rehab; sending hospital has no inpatient rehab unit.
Patient requires transfer to another facility.
Family prefers the rehab facility.

questions.explain: Payers use this box to judge whether the patient went to the right place. Name the service the sending facility doesn't have.
questions.source: GMR End User IMT: Interfacility Transport Justification; Clinical Documentation Requirements

questions.prompt: For Medicare, a patient is 'bed-confined' when they are…

options.text: Unable to walk without help, and in bed most of the day
Unable to walk OR unable to sit in a chair
Unable to get up from bed without help, unable to walk, AND unable to sit in a chair or wheelchair
Lying in a hospital bed when you arrive

questions.explain: All three must be true. If the patient can sit in a wheelchair, they aren't bed-confined, even if they can't walk.
questions.source: 42 CFR §410.40 (bed-confined definition)

questions.prompt: Writing 'Pt bedbound' is enough to show the patient needed an ambulance.
questions.explain: 'Bedbound' is a label, and reviewers discount it. Chart each of the three criteria and what you saw: how they moved, what help it took, what happened when they tried to sit.

questions.prompt: A signed PCS doesn't, by itself, prove the transport was medically necessary.
questions.explain: Medicare says the signed certification alone doesn't show medical necessity. Your chart has to back it up with the patient's condition.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a medical reason for an ambulance?

options.text: No wheelchair van was available, and the appointment couldn't be moved
The family asked for an ambulance
The patient prefers the stretcher
Hip contractures keep the patient from sitting; 2-person lift to cot

questions.explain: Availability, convenience and preference aren't medical reasons. Chart the condition that made a seated ride unsafe.
questions.source: 42 CFR §410.40 (other means of transport contraindicated)

questions.context: 74-year-old, 3 days after left hip repair, going from the hospital to rehab.
questions.quote: PT TRANSPORTED BY STRETCHER FOR SAFETY.
questions.prompt: What's the best way to chart this?

options.text: Can't get OOB without 2 assist, can't bear weight on L leg, can't sit up >5 min d/t surgical pain 7/10.
Pt bed-confined, stretcher required for safety.
Pt is a fall risk; facility requested stretcher transport.
Pt recovering from hip surgery, transported by stretcher.

questions.explain: The right answer covers all three bed-confined criteria with what you actually saw. 'For safety', 'fall risk' and 'bed-confined' are conclusions without the evidence.

questions.context: BLS transfer from the hospital to a skilled nursing facility.
questions.prompt: Tap the line a reviewer would use to deny the claim.

narrative.text: Pt supine in bed, states "I can't sit up, my back hurts."
Pt ambulated to the cot with standby assist.
Moved to bed at SNF by draw sheet, 2 assist.

questions.explain: If the patient walked to the cot, the chart has to say why a seated ride wasn't safe. Walking doesn't rule out an ambulance, but it has to be explained.

questions.context: You're driving past two closer hospitals. The MNC worksheet asks: closest appropriate facility?
questions.prompt: What do you chart?

options.text: 'Yes', because the doctor picked it
'No', and name the service the closer hospitals don't offer
Leave it blank
'No', because the family prefers the farther hospital

questions.explain: Medicare generally pays mileage only to the nearest facility that can give the needed care. Name the specific service; family preference isn't a reason.
questions.source: GMR End User IMT: PCS and MNC; Medicare closest-appropriate-facility rule

questions.prompt: Medical necessity depends on today's condition, not the diagnosis alone.
questions.explain: 'Hip fracture' doesn't tell a reviewer why today's patient couldn't sit. Chart what you found today.

questions.context: At pickup, the PCS is blank.
questions.prompt: What do you do?

options.text: Sign it yourself as the crew
Leave and chart 'PCS not available'
Ask the facility to have the physician or other authorized staff complete and sign it
Have the patient sign it

questions.explain: Crews can't certify medical necessity; if the physician isn't available, a PA, NP, clinical nurse specialist, RN or discharge planner who knows the patient can sign. Take a clear photo for the chart.
questions.source: 42 CFR §410.40 (who may sign); GMR End User IMT: Trailing Documents

questions.context: Patient on home oxygen going to a dialysis appointment.
questions.quote: PT ON HOME O2, AMBULANCE REQUIRED.
questions.prompt: What's the best way to chart this?

options.text: Pt on O2, can't go by wheelchair van.
Pt on oxygen; transported per protocol.
Pt O2 dependent, stretcher needed.
On home O2 2 L NC. SpO2 87% and RR 28 when HOB raised >45°; can't tolerate sitting up.

questions.explain: Many home-oxygen patients ride seated with their own tank. Show what made sitting unsafe: the numbers and what you saw.
